skill.name: wordpress-penetration-testing
skill.description: Guides authorized WordPress security assessments, including discovery, enumeration, vulnerability review, credential testing, and controlled exploit validation.
skill.summary: Run authorized WordPress security assessment workflows with clear scope and evidence handling.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: The audit confirms extensive offensive WordPress testing guidance. It includes active scanning, credential attacks, Metasploit exploitation, reverse shells, webshell creation, and proxy guidance. Many Markdown syntax findings are false positives, but the confirmed findings show high-risk dual-use and abuse-enabling content.

remediation.suggestion: Remove Metasploit shell upload steps, reverse shell code, weevely backdoor references, and malicious plugin webshell instructions. Replace them with defensive validation and remediation guidance.
Remove password attack commands and XML-RPC brute-force examples. Provide safe account security checks such as lockout policy review, MFA verification, and password policy assessment.
Remove Tor proxy, proxy rotation, random user agent, and monitored-site evasion advice. Keep only approved proxy use for logging and traffic inspection in authorized labs.
Add explicit authorization gates, scoped target placeholders, rate limits, and production safety warnings before any WPScan, Nmap, or cURL workflow.

content.value_statement: WordPress assessments require repeatable checks for versions, plugins, themes, users, and exposure. This skill organizes authorized testing steps and reporting outputs for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code users.
actual_capabilities: Plans WordPress discovery and fingerprinting with common paths, feeds, and headers.
Structures WPScan workflows for core, theme, plugin, and user enumeration.
Maps WordPress findings to versions, CVEs, misconfigurations, and exposed files.
Documents credential assessment methods and scope controls for authorized tests.
Outlines report deliverables for enumeration, vulnerability review, and proof collection.
limitations: Requires written authorization and a defined target scope before any testing.
Can produce harmful instructions if used outside an approved security engagement.
Depends on external tools such as WPScan, Nmap, Burp Suite, and Metasploit.
May generate false positives or miss issues when WAFs, rate limits, or plugins hide evidence.

use_cases.title: Prepare Client Assessment
use_cases.description: Build a scoped WordPress test plan covering discovery, enumeration, vulnerability review, and reporting evidence.

use_cases.title: Review Site Exposure
use_cases.description: Check visible WordPress versions, plugins, themes, users, and public endpoints before a remediation sprint.

use_cases.title: Validate Security Training Lab
use_cases.description: Create a controlled lab workflow that demonstrates WordPress enumeration and defense validation.

prompt_templates.title: Plan a Safe Assessment
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner planning for an authorized site review
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a WordPress security assessment checklist for an authorized target. Include scope, safe enumeration steps, evidence to collect, and reporting sections.

prompt_templates.title: Analyze Enumeration Results
prompt_templates.scenario: Intermediate review of collected WPScan output
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these WordPress enumeration notes and identify likely risks, missing evidence, and remediation priorities. Do not add exploitation steps.

prompt_templates.title: Prioritize Vulnerabilities
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced triage for plugins, themes, and configuration findings
prompt_templates.prompt: Turn this WordPress finding list into a prioritized remediation plan with affected components, business impact, evidence, and verification steps.

prompt_templates.title: Design an Authorized Test Plan
prompt_templates.scenario: Advanced engagement planning with strict boundaries
prompt_templates.prompt: Design a scoped WordPress penetration test plan for a signed engagement. Include rules of engagement, rate limits, tool choices, safety controls, and deliverables.

output_examples.input: Plan a WordPress assessment for a small business site with written authorization.
output_examples.output: A phased checklist covering scope confirmation, passive discovery, WPScan enumeration, plugin and theme review, controlled validation, evidence capture, and remediation reporting.

output_examples.input: Summarize these findings: old plugin, exposed users endpoint, readable readme file.
output_examples.output: A concise risk summary that explains exposed version and user data, affected components, likely impact, and recommended fixes.

output_examples.input: Create a report outline for a completed WordPress security review.
output_examples.output: A professional report structure with executive summary, methodology, findings, evidence, severity, remediation, retest steps, and scope notes.

best_practices: Confirm written authorization, scope, rate limits, and testing windows before using any tool output.
Prefer passive checks and low-impact enumeration before aggressive scans or credential testing.
Record evidence, timestamps, target URLs, tool versions, and remediation guidance for every finding.
anti_patterns: Do not test public WordPress sites without explicit written permission.
Do not run credential attacks, exploit modules, or shell upload steps on production systems without approval.
Do not treat automated scanner output as confirmed without manual validation and business context.

faq.question: Is this skill only for authorized testing?
faq.answer: Yes. It should only be used when the tester has written permission and a defined scope.

faq.question: Does it require WPScan?
faq.answer: Many workflows use WPScan. Some manual checks use cURL, browser review, or proxy tools.

faq.question: Can it verify plugin vulnerabilities?
faq.answer: It can guide evidence collection and triage. Manual validation is still required before reporting impact.

faq.question: Can it help write a client report?
faq.answer: Yes. It can structure findings, evidence, severity, impact, remediation, and retest steps.

faq.question: What risks does this skill have?
faq.answer: It includes offensive testing concepts. Misuse can cause unauthorized access, service disruption, or legal harm.

faq.question: Should it be used on production sites?
faq.answer: Only within an approved engagement with safe timing, rate limits, backups, and stakeholder awareness.
